title: Get them to behave with no skills whatsoever: Part 1 - Narrate What You See
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles launches a practical behavior management series by presenting a single high-leverage technique that any teacher—even an NQT on their first day—can use immediately with immediate effect: narrating what you see. After giving a clear written instruction and waiting 30 seconds, the teacher walks the rows calling out line counts aloud (3 lines, 1 line, 0 lines) without commentary, praise, or engagement. The technique creates social comparison that students respond to faster and more reliably than teacher-imposed expectations, because peer norms are far more powerful than adult authority. No one wants to appear last or least productive in front of their peers, so behavior improves without relationship capital, emotional regulation, trauma-informed practice, or any other skill. Salles is explicit that he is not dismissing those things—they matter—but this is a toolbox, not a character-development guide. The technique works because it's anonymous (everyone gets counted), it's mathematical (not evaluative), and its effect is cumulative: repeated twice or three times, it installs a new social norm where writing more is the default expectation driven by peers, not the teacher.
points: The most powerful driver of student behavior is peer norms, not teacher authority: calling out line counts creates social comparison that motivates students faster and more reliably than any praise, reminder, or relationship-based technique.

The key mechanism is removing external excuses: a student who hears '0 lines' called out cannot tell themselves 'I don't get it'—they feel visible and respond to protect their social standing among peers.

This technique requires zero skill but precise execution: it fails when the teacher breaks the count to engage in conversation, when instructions aren't written down, when they lose courage and skip a student with 0 lines, or when they don't repeat it at least 2-3 times.

Repetition is what makes it a social norm rather than a one-time trick: after three uses, students compete with each other to write more, and writing hard becomes what the class does, not what the teacher demands.

The technique works regardless of the teacher's relationship with the class or their emotional state, making it especially valuable for new teachers, classes with difficult dynamics, or any context where standard behavior management hasn't taken hold.
quotes: Everything I'll show you, an ECT could do tomorrow, with instant impact. You don't have to watch your emotions, and be the adult in the room. You don't have to go out of your way to build great relationships. You don't have to be trauma informed.

During your 30 second wait, you are scanning for the end of rows. You are looking for the student who has written most. Then you position yourself in front of that desk, and start calling out a count. 3 lines. 1 line. 0 lines. 2 lines. 1 line. No chatting, no comments, no words of encouragement, no questions. Just count.
No student can tell themselves 'I don't get it', 'this is hard', 'I'll just chill till the teacher notices me'. They can have no external excuses.
No student wants to appear stupid. 0 lines will hurt them. So will 1. They will want to compete with their friends, or they will fear being last.

New numbers get increasingly higher, and these turn a greater number of lines written into a social norm. Social norms which come from peers are way, way easier to establish than social norms teachers try to impose.
Students who work well, pay attention, and don't look for distractions have instant kudos. Nothing is done for the teacher's approval - it is for peer approval. That's your super-power.
